texts.period: Inuit oral tradition (West Greenland); collected by Knud Rasmussen, published 1921

source.work: Knud Rasmussen (collector), Eskimo Folk-Tales, ed. and rendered into English by W. J. Alexander Worster (Gyldendal, 1921), 'The Eagle and the Whale', eBook #28932

summary.en: Taunted with 'an eagle you shall have' and 'a whale you shall have,' two refusing sisters are each carried off by exactly that husband — the eagle to a high cliff ledge, the whale to a rock. Both plait sinew lines to escape; the brothers kill the eagle with crossbows (the smallest homeless boy's arrow strikes first), and rescue the whale's wife by sea: she ties her restraining string to a stone, and as the pursuing whale closes on their umiak she throws out hairband, mittens, lining, frock, and coat, each swallowed in a burst of foam — the last thing, her breeches, buys them the shore, and the whale is cast up as a sun-bleached bone.
summary.zh: 兄弟戲言『那就讓鷹娶你』『那就讓鯨娶你』，兩位拒婚的姊妹果真被鷹與鯨各自擄走。二人皆編筋索謀逃；兄弟們以弩射殺鷹夫——最小孤兒一箭先中。鯨妻則將拴她的繩繫於石上逃歸；鯨追大舟時，她依次擲出髮帶、手套、手套內襯、外衣、內衣，鯨逐件撲吞，泡沫翻騰；最後一件褲子為船贏得海岸，鯨擱淺為一副日曬白骨。

sensitivity.note: West Greenland tale recorded by Rasmussen, 1910s. Animal-husband (bird/whale) type tale; cross-tradition parallel to star-husband and animal-bridegroom tales.

passages.text: In a certain village many brothers had two sisters, both of an age to marry, whom they often urged to take husbands, but the sisters would not. At last one of the men said: 'What sort of a husband do you want, then? An eagle, perhaps? Very well, an eagle you shall have' — and to the other: 'And you perhaps would like a whale? Well, a whale you shall have.' Suddenly a great eagle swooped down on the one girl and flew off with her to a high ledge of rock, and a whale came and carried off the other sister likewise. The eagle and his wife lived on a ledge far up a steep cliff; he flew out over the sea to hunt, sometimes appearing with a walrus in one claw and a narwhal in the other, while his wife plaited sinews for a line wherewith to lower herself down the rock — and one day, trying the line, found it too short, and plaited more.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Knud Rasmussen, Eskimo Folk-Tales (Worster 1921), 'The Eagle and the Whale'; not verbatim.

passages.text: The brothers, longing for their sister, set to work making crossbows, and among them a little homeless boy so small he had not strength to draw a bow, but must get another to draw it for him every time he wanted to shoot. When all was ready they called to her from the foot of the cliff, and as soon as her husband had gone hunting she lowered herself down. Towards evening the eagle appeared out at sea with a walrus in each claw, dropped one down to the brothers, found his wife gone, threw his catch away, and came gliding on widespread wings — but whenever he tried to fly down to the house they shot at him, and none could hit, until the little homeless boy cried 'Let me try too!'; another bent his bow for him, the arrow struck, and as the eagle fluttered down the others shot so many arrows into it that it could not quite touch the ground. Thus they killed their sister's husband, who was a mighty hunter.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Knud Rasmussen, Eskimo Folk-Tales (Worster 1921), 'The Eagle and the Whale'; not verbatim.

passages.text: The other sister and the whale lived together likewise, the whale so fond of her he would hardly let her out of his sight; she too grew homesick and plaited her sinew line, and her brothers, testing their new-built umiak against a flying guillemot, took the too-slow boat to pieces and built a swift one that beat the bird. When the girl said 'I must go outside a little,' the whale pulled the string tied to her; 'I am only just outside the passage,' she cried — and tied the string to a stone, running down the hill while the whale hauled at the stone thinking it his wife.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Knud Rasmussen, Eskimo Folk-Tales (Worster 1921), 'The Eagle and the Whale'; not verbatim.

passages.text: The brothers fled with her in the umiak, and the whale rolled out into the sea and overhauled them, seeming to make the boat stand still. 'Throw out your hairband' — the sea foamed up and the whale stopped; 'Throw out one of your mittens,' then the mitten's lining, her outer frock, her inner coat — each pounced on in a burst of foam, the boat closer and closer to land — 'Throw out your breeches!' The sea lashed into foam, the umiak reached the land, and the whale, trying to follow, was cast up on the shore as a white and sun-bleached bone of a whale.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Knud Rasmussen, Eskimo Folk-Tales (Worster 1921), 'The Eagle and the Whale'; not verbatim.

title.en: The Two Little Outcasts and the House That Vanished
title.zh: 兩名棄兒與消失的小屋

texts.period: Inuit oral tradition (West Greenland); collected by Knud Rasmussen, published 1921

source.work: Knud Rasmussen (collector), Eskimo Folk-Tales, ed. and rendered into English by W. J. Alexander Worster (Gyldendal, 1921), 'The two little Outcasts', eBook #28932

summary.en: Two orphan boys, whose ptarmigan catches are always taken from them, find in a ravine a fox-skin-covered little house where a lone boy plays kayak-man with a cutting-board; his giant mother returns with a load on her back, feeds them marvelously, and buys one of their arrow-sets with meat enough to carry. Warned — 'Do not let any others come selling arrows' — the villagers go anyway the next day, and the house in the ravine is gone: not a stone, not a shed, no trace of the woman; and that was the last time the boys went out hunting ptarmigan.
summary.zh: 兩名父母雙亡的男孩天天獵雷鳥，獵物卻總被村人奪走。某日他們在峽谷底發現一所覆著藍白狐皮的小屋，屋中獨童以切肉板為皮艇、木棍為槳玩耍；其巨婦之母負重而歸，款待他們，並以滿背肉食購下他們一副箭。臨別告誡：『別讓別人也來賣箭。』村民不聽，次日全都背箭前往——谷中那屋已消失無蹤：不見片瓦、不見棚屋、不見婦人。從此男孩們再也不去獵雷鳥。

sensitivity.note: West Greenland tale recorded by Rasmussen, 1910s. The non-human household is a standard Greenlandic otherworld encounter.

passages.text: There were two little boys who had no father and no mother, and went out every day hunting ptarmigan with no weapons save a bow — and the men of the place were always eager to take their catch. One day, finding no ptarmigan, they came to wild difficult cliffs and looked down into a ravine at something that looked like a stone: a little house. Climbing on the roof and looking down through the air hole, they saw a little boy on the floor with a cutting-board for a kayak and a stick for a paddle, playing at being a man in a kayak; twice they called to him before he ran to hide, and they found him inside, sobbing a little, pressing himself close against the wall. 'Do you live here all alone?' 'No, my mother went out early this morning, and she is out now, as usual.' 'We have come to be here with you because you are all alone,' they said, and he ventured out from the wall.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Knud Rasmussen, Eskimo Folk-Tales (Worster 1921), 'The two little Outcasts'; not verbatim.

passages.text: Toward evening the boy said, 'Now I can see her, away to the south' — and they saw a mighty big figure with something on her back coming quickly nearer, throwing down her burden with a great noise. She came in hot and tired: 'Thanks, kind little boys. I had to leave him alone in the house, as usual, and now you have stayed with him while I was fearing for him on my way.' She brought dried flesh of fox and reindeer and a big piece of suet, and the fox meat proved wonderfully good to eat. The little boy whispered in her ear — he had a great desire for one of their sets of arrows — and they gave it. When the outcasts set off home, she paid them with as much meat as they could carry and warned them: 'Be sure you do not let any others come selling arrows.'
passages.note: Paraphrase of Knud Rasmussen, Eskimo Folk-Tales (Worster 1921), 'The two little Outcasts'; not verbatim.

passages.text: The village received the returning boys with astonishment at their load; the food was wonderfully good to eat. 'That we were given in payment for one set of arrows,' they said. 'We must certainly go out and sell arrows, too,' said the others, and although the two told them the warning — 'Do not let any others come selling arrows' — all fell to making arrows at once and set out the next day, the little outcasts going in despite of their desire, because the others ordered them. When they came to the ravine, the house was no longer there: not a stone of it, not the two sheds, nothing; and no one could tell where that woman had gone. And that was the last time they went out hunting ptarmigan.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Knud Rasmussen, Eskimo Folk-Tales (Worster 1921), 'The two little Outcasts'; not verbatim.

texts.period: Inuit oral tradition (West Greenland); collected by Knud Rasmussen, published 1921

source.work: Knud Rasmussen (collector), Eskimo Folk-Tales, ed. and rendered into English by W. J. Alexander Worster (Gyldendal, 1921), 'Atdlarneq, the great glutton', eBook #28932

summary.en: The strongman Atdlarneq, who never failed to catch a seal, loiters south instead and finds a house where three yellow-seamed women come out one by one — and their master, whose cheeks are made of copper, smells him the moment he hides. Forced to eat a sack of fish, half a black seal's blubber, the frozen half, and a whole seal, drinking the water bucket to the last drop, he survives thanks to a swallowed grass stalk that made room — and never goes southward again.
summary.zh: 從不失手的力士阿德勒涅克這天卻沿岸南游，撞見一戶人家——三名黃色滾邊的婦人一一出屋，她們的銅腮主人一下便嗅出躲藏的他，逼他吃光一袋魚、半扇黑海豹油脂、凍肉半扇、整隻海豹，喝乾水桶。幸而他開吃前吞了一根草莖騰出胃袋，才沒被撐死。自此他再也不敢南行。

sensitivity.note: West Greenland tale recorded by Rasmussen, 1910s. Copper-cheeks (Qerreripag) is a bogey figure of Greenlandic folklore, per the source's note.

passages.text: Atdlarneq was a strong man: if he rowed but a little way out in his kayak he caught a seal, and was never content with only one. But one day, instead of hunting seal, he paddled close along the shore making south, and sighted a little house on the sunny side of a cape. A woman came out — a yellow band round her hair, yellow seams to all her clothes — and he waited for another; another came out, the same; then a third, quite like the others, bearing a dish in her hand. Then at last he went on shore, and they received him very kindly, bringing great quantities of food.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Knud Rasmussen, Eskimo Folk-Tales (Worster 1921), 'Atdlarneq, the great glutton'; not verbatim.

passages.text: In the evening the three women began going outside again and again, and when he asked why, all answered at once: 'It is because we now expect our dear master home.' Afraid, Atdlarneq hid behind the skin hangings — and the master came, his cheeks made of copper, sniffing: 'Hum! There is a smell of people here.' Crawling out, he was received eagerly: 'Has he had nothing to eat yet? Then bring food at once.' A sack full of fish and a big piece of blubber from the half of a black seal, and a violent command: 'You are to eat this all up, and if you do not eat it all up, I will thrash you with my copper cheeks!' He chewed and chewed, ate it all up, drank the water bucket to the last drop, then ate the frozen half-seal, then a whole black seal, until there was no more left, and again emptied the bucket.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Knud Rasmussen, Eskimo Folk-Tales (Worster 1921), 'Atdlarneq, the great glutton'; not verbatim.

passages.text: After all that he felt very well indeed, and seemed hardly to have eaten until now — because he had swallowed a little stalk of grass before he began, which made room in him. So Atdlarneq slept, and next morning went back home; but after having thus nearly gorged himself to death, he never went southward again.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Knud Rasmussen, Eskimo Folk-Tales (Worster 1921), 'Atdlarneq, the great glutton'; not verbatim.

title.en: Angangujuk, Lost to the Inland Folk
title.zh: 安甘古茹克被內陸人抱走

texts.period: Inuit oral tradition (Godthaab, West Greenland); collected by Knud Rasmussen, published 1921

source.work: Knud Rasmussen (collector), Eskimo Folk-Tales, ed. and rendered into English by W. J. Alexander Worster (Gyldendal, 1921), 'Angangujuk', eBook #28932

summary.en: Playing kayak-man in the passage, little Angangujuk vanishes from his mother's callings. His furious father blames her, hunts down wizards, and at last finds a spirit-finder who sends word: the child is up between two great cliffs, in the care of two old inland folk. Journeying east, they come on smoking houses where the tornit quarrel over who shall keep the boy; a magic sleep is called down sleeper by sleeper until the last yawns, the child is snatched (his clothes poked down with poles from the high drying frame), and the umiak rows for the farthest islands while the inlanders beat their own house down in fury.
summary.zh: 小安甘古茹克在甬道裡扮演皮艇手，忽然應聲消失。父親遷怒母親，遍訪巫師，終得通靈者指路：孩子就在兩座巨崖之間，由兩名內陸老人照看。一行東行至炊煙裊裊的屋群——托尼特人正為誰撫養孩子爭執不休。巫師逐一施下沉睡咒，連最後一人也打呵欠倒下；父親奪回赤身的兒子，晾架太高，須用長杆把衣裳捅下來。大舟疾駛遠島，內陸人怒而拆屋。自此他們再不住大陸。

sensitivity.note: Godthaab district tale recorded by Rasmussen, 1910s. The inland-folk child-stealing motif is presented as told in the source.

passages.text: Angangujuk's father was very strong, and the three of them lived alone without other neighbours. One day the mother, scraping meat from a skin, let the child play at kayak outside in the passage, near the entrance, calling to him now and again: 'Angangujuk!' — and the child answered from outside. Once there came no answer; she left the skin and searched about, but could not find the child, and began to feel greatly afraid, dreading her husband's return. When he came out from behind a rock dragging a seal, he asked where their little son was, and on her answer — that he had vanished while playing kayak-man in the passage — he answered: 'It is you, wicked old hag, who have killed him. And now I will kill you.' She begged him to wait and first seek out one who could ask counsel of the spirits; he brought home wizards, and let them go without so much as a bite of meat when they could not find the child.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Knud Rasmussen, Eskimo Folk-Tales (Worster 1921), 'Angangujuk'; not verbatim.

passages.text: At last he found a very clever finder of hidden things, fastened a stick to his face, and made him lie on the bedplace working until the spirit came. The spirit finder declared: 'It would seem that spirits have here found a difficult task. He is up in a place between two great cliffs, and two old inland folk are looking after him.' They wandered away towards the east until they sighted many houses with smoke coming out of all the smoke holes; through the window the father saw they were quarrelling about his child, who was crying, each one eager to have him. Asked what he would like to eat, the child refused everything; asked if he wanted to go home very much, Angangujuk answered quickly: 'Yes.'
passages.note: Paraphrase of Knud Rasmussen, Eskimo Folk-Tales (Worster 1921), 'Angangujuk'; not verbatim.

passages.text: 'Try now to magic them to sleep,' said the father, and the wizard began calling down a magic sleep upon those in the hut, one by one sinking to sleep and snoring, until only two remained awake; then one yawned and rolled over, and at last the great finder of hidden things called down sleep with all his might over the last one, who also rolled over. Angangujuk's father went in quickly and caught up his son — naked; his clothes hung on a drying frame so high they had to poke them down with poles. They came out, walked far, cut the moorings of the umiak, and rowed out to the farthest islands; the inland folk, seeing them gone, went up to the house and beat down roof and walls and all there was of it. After that time Angangujuk's parents never again took up their dwelling on the mainland.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Knud Rasmussen, Eskimo Folk-Tales (Worster 1921), 'Angangujuk'; not verbatim.

title.zh: 阿塔舒亞克之子：海豹皮泳者

texts.period: Inuit oral tradition (Godthaab, West Greenland); collected by Knud Rasmussen, published 1921

source.work: Knud Rasmussen (collector), Eskimo Folk-Tales, ed. and rendered into English by W. J. Alexander Worster (Gyldendal, 1921), 'Atarssuaq', eBook #28932

summary.en: Unable to be killed by his many enemies, Atarssuaq trains his newborn son by daily dunkings, then in a fjord-seal skin dried like a bladder; the boy becomes so clever a diver his father weeps for fear of sharks. When the enemies kill Atarssuaq and many kayaks come north to finish the family, the boy lures them out to sea by surfacing and vanishing, climbs a grounded iceberg, topples each wave of climbers with a great piece of ice, drowns the kayaks, and spares the last — a weeping man armed with only a fish-killing stick — with a warning never to come again.
summary.zh: 仇人殺不死阿塔舒亞克，他便把新生兒日日拋水練泳，再讓他穿上如膀胱般晾乾的海豹皮；少年潛水之巧，令父親一度哭怕鯊魚。父親被害後，北方大隊皮艇來襲，少年時隱時現誘其出海，攀上擱淺冰山，以巨冰逐一砸落攀爬者，又拽翻皮艇、按人入水。最後一名——只持殺魚棍、泣不成聲的男子——被他放回，並留下警告：再來者無一生還。

sensitivity.note: Godthaab district tale recorded by Rasmussen, 1910s. Killing raid presented as told in the source.

passages.text: Atarssuaq had many enemies who tried in vain to hurt him, for they could not kill him. When his wife bore him a son, he bore the child down to the water and threw him in, waited until he kicked out violently, and took him up again — doing so every day for long after while the child grew, so that the boy became a very clever swimmer. Atarssuaq once caught a fjord seal, took off the skin all in one piece, dried it like a bladder, and made his son put it on when he went swimming. To see how clever the boy had become, he followed him out to sea in his kayak, the boy swimming more and more under water, disappearing each time the father raised his throwing stick; sent to keep under water as much as he could for a long way, the boy stayed down so long that the father, afraid, had just begun to cry — 'If only the sharks have not found him!' — when his son came up again, and they went in to land.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Knud Rasmussen, Eskimo Folk-Tales (Worster 1921), 'Atarssuaq'; not verbatim.

passages.text: One day his father did not come back from hunting, because his enemies had killed him. Evening came, and next morning a kayak from the north put in: 'To-morrow the many brothers will come to kill you all' — and turned at once and went back. In the morning many kayaks appeared from the northward, and the boy, told by his mother to put on his swimming dress, went down to the shore, close to the water; the kayaks rowed towards him saying he had fallen in, searched about for him, and he came up just in front of the bone shoeing on the nose of one kayak, dived down again, and so led all those kayaks out to the open sea. There he sighted a grounded iceberg, climbed it by sticking his hands into the ice, heard them propose to cut steps up to him, and waited until the head of the foremost came over the edge before letting fall a great piece of ice that sent them all down; again they crawled up, again the ice fell, and all who had climbed on were killed, lured on by him.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Knud Rasmussen, Eskimo Folk-Tales (Worster 1921), 'Atarssuaq'; not verbatim.

passages.text: The others turned back, saying he would kill them all if they did not go; the boy jumped down, swam to the kayaks, and began tugging at their paddles till they turned over, the men righting themselves with their throwing sticks, until he was forced to hold them down himself under water till they drowned. Of all those many kayaks only one was left, a man with no weapon but a stick for killing fish, who rowed weeping in towards land.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Knud Rasmussen, Eskimo Folk-Tales (Worster 1921), 'Atarssuaq'; not verbatim.

passages.text: The boy pulled the paddle away from him, and the man began paddling with his hands; the boy gripped his hands from below until he dared no longer put them in the water at all, weeping greatly: 'It is ill for me that ever I came out on this errand, for it is plain that I am to be killed.' The boy looked at him a little, and said: 'You I will not kill. You may go home again' — giving back his paddle and calling after him: 'Tell those of your place never to come out again thinking to kill us. For if they do not one of them will return alive.' None ever came against them after that time.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Knud Rasmussen, Eskimo Folk-Tales (Worster 1921), 'Atarssuaq'; not verbatim.

title.zh: 普瓦克舒克與吹哨訪客

texts.period: Inuit oral tradition (Godthaab, West Greenland); collected by Knud Rasmussen, published 1921

source.work: Knud Rasmussen (collector), Eskimo Folk-Tales, ed. and rendered into English by W. J. Alexander Worster (Gyldendal, 1921), 'Puagssuaq', eBook #28932

summary.en: A wifeless ptarmigan-hunter finds in a rocky valley a house like a stone where an old couple sits alone. He whistles twice; the husband nudges his wife — 'You, Puagssuaq, you can talk with the spirits' — then, at the third whistle, decides the sound is 'the voice of a shore-dweller; one who catches miserable fish.' The wife lets down her hair to call the spirits, and the passage way begins closing around the unseen visitor; it opens of itself, he slips out, and runs the whole hillside home without ever being pursued.
summary.zh: 以獵雷鳥為生的無妻者誤入巖谷中一所石屋般的小屋，屋內一對老夫婦獨坐。他吹了兩聲口哨，老翁推了推老伴：『普瓦克舒克，你能通靈，快去問問。』第三聲哨響，老翁凝神道：『聽！倒像是海濱人的聲音——一個只會捕可憐小魚的傢伙。』老嫗披髮欲召靈，甬道已無聲收攏，將合未合之際忽然自開，他趁隙溜出，一路狂奔上山——竟無人追來。

sensitivity.note: Godthaab district tale recorded by Rasmussen, 1910s. Whistling as spirit-call is a documented Greenlandic practice.

passages.text: There was once a wifeless man who always went out hunting ptarmigan, every day. One day, from a place whence he could see out over a rocky valley that looked good to go into, he went down; before he had come to the bottom he caught sight of something that looked like a stone — and when he could see quite clearly it was not a stone at all, he walked up to it. Looking in, he saw an old couple sitting alone inside; he crawled very silently in through the passage way, looked at them a long time, and gave a little whistle. Nothing happened, so he whistled a second time, and now they heard it: the man nudged his wife and said, 'You, Puagssuaq, you can talk with the spirits. Take counsel with them now.'
passages.note: Paraphrase of Knud Rasmussen, Eskimo Folk-Tales (Worster 1921), 'Puagssuaq'; not verbatim.

passages.text: At the third whistle the old man looked at his wife again and said earnestly: 'Listen! It sounds as if that might be the voice of a shore-dweller; one who catches miserable fish.' The wifeless man saw the old woman letting down her hair, because she was about to ask counsel of the spirits — and then saw the passage way about him beginning to close up, already nearly closed. But then it opened again of itself; thinking only of coming out from that place, he slipped out when it opened, and began running as fast as he could. For a long time he ran on, with the thought that someone would surely come after him — but he came up the hillside without having been pursued at all, went home, and told what had happened.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Knud Rasmussen, Eskimo Folk-Tales (Worster 1921), 'Puagssuaq'; not verbatim.

title.en: Tungujuluk and Saunikoq: The Bear and the Walrus
title.zh: 通古茹盧克與薩烏尼洛克：熊與海象

texts.period: Inuit oral tradition (Godthaab, West Greenland); collected by Knud Rasmussen, published 1921

source.work: Knud Rasmussen (collector), Eskimo Folk-Tales, ed. and rendered into English by W. J. Alexander Worster (Gyldendal, 1921), 'Tungujuluk and Saunikoq', eBook #28932

summary.en: Two village wizards, one turning bear at spirit-callings and the other walrus. Childless Saunikoq, jealous of Tungujuluk's kayaking son, stalks the boy in bearskin — and laughs away the father's knife just in time. Tungujuluk waits many days, then takes walrus shape himself, lets Saunikoq harpoon him, folds the bladder float under his arm, and rows home to hold a meat feast where he lays the recovered bladder and line beside the dish: 'Aha, at last I have paid you for the time when you came in the shape of a bear, and mocked us.' Saunikoq rows north in his umiak and is never seen again, so great was his shame.
summary.zh: 同村兩巫師：降靈時一化熊、一化海象。膝下無子的薩烏尼洛克妒忌通古茹盧克會划艇的兒子，披熊皮暗伏欲殺——父親舉刀之際，熊開口大笑，他才認出是鄰人，強自收刀。多日後，通古茹盧克自化海象，任其叉中，挾浮囊而泳歸，設宴將浮囊繩線擺在肉盤旁：『啊哈，你扮熊來嘲弄我們的帳，今日總算還清。』滿座大笑；薩烏尼洛克羞愧難當，次日清早駕大舟北去，從此無人再見。

sensitivity.note: Godthaab district tale recorded by Rasmussen, 1910s. Wizard shape-shifting (bear/walrus skins) is documented angakok practice.

passages.text: Tungujuluk and Saunikoq were men from one village, and both were wizards: when they heard a spirit calling, one would change into a bear, and the other into a walrus. Tungujuluk had a son, but Saunikoq had no children; and as soon as the boy was old enough, Tungujuluk taught him to paddle a kayak, at which Saunikoq grew jealous and began planning evil. One morning he went out hunting seal as usual, went up to an island, called for his bearskin, got into it, and moved off towards Tungujuluk's house, landing a little way off and stealing up to kill the son — not knowing the father had already come home and was sitting busily at work on the kayak he was making for his boy.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Knud Rasmussen, Eskimo Folk-Tales (Worster 1921), 'Tungujuluk and Saunikoq'; not verbatim.

passages.text: Just as the big bear came close, the boy went weeping home to his father, who looked round, took a knife, and ran towards it, about to stab — when it began to laugh. Tungujuluk remembered that his neighbour Saunikoq was able to take the shape of a bear, and was now so angry that he had nearly stabbed him in spite of all, holding back his knife only with difficulty. But he did not forget. Many days later he went out in his kayak, went up on an island, called his other shape to him, crawled into it, and became a walrus; then he went where it was the custom for kayaks to hunt seal, rose to the surface quite near Saunikoq, made himself small, and crept over to one side of the skin so the stroke could not fail. Struck, he floundered but not too violently lest he break the line, swam away under water with the bladder float, folded it up under his arm, took out the air, and swam in to land near where his kayak lay.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Knud Rasmussen, Eskimo Folk-Tales (Worster 1921), 'Tungujuluk and Saunikoq'; not verbatim.

passages.text: He took the harpoon point out, went out hunting, struck a black seal, rowed home at once, and made his wife cook the breast piece; when the other kayaks came home he made a meat feast, and Saunikoq, thinking nothing of any matter, came in with the others. They ate and were satisfied, and each man told of his day's hunting, until Saunikoq said: 'To-day, when I struck a walrus, I did not think at all that it should cause me to lose my bladder float. Where that came up again is a thing we do not know. That bladder float of mine was lost.' Then Tungujuluk took the bladder and line from his kayak, laid them beside the meat dish, and said: 'Whose can this bladder be, now, I wonder? Aha, at last I have paid you for the time when you came in the shape of a bear, and mocked us.' The many who sat there laughed greatly; Saunikoq got up and went away, and next morning very early set out and rowed northward in his umiak, and since then he has not been seen — so great a shame did he feel.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Knud Rasmussen, Eskimo Folk-Tales (Worster 1921), 'Tungujuluk and Saunikoq'; not verbatim.

title.en: Anarteq, Who Became a Salmon and Came Back

texts.period: Inuit oral tradition (Godthaab, West Greenland); collected by Knud Rasmussen, published 1921

source.work: Knud Rasmussen (collector), Eskimo Folk-Tales, ed. and rendered into English by W. J. Alexander Worster (Gyldendal, 1921), 'Anarteq', eBook #28932

summary.en: Drowned playing with a reindeer calf he had struck in the lake, Anarteq wakes as a salmon; his old father, left to hunt like a young man, returns years later to the abandoned fjord and weeps for his son. The salmon coming up from the sea takes hold of the father's steering paddle — twice, the second time so the slow raising of the paddle draws the son up with it — and Anarteq becomes a man again, hunting many years to feed his kin.
summary.zh: 阿納特克在湖中戲弄被自己擊中的馴鹿幼崽，反被踢翻皮艇溺斃，醒來已化身鮭魚。老父失去獨子，只得像年輕人般親自出獵，多年後重返故地，峽灣深處垂淚思子。海中隨群而上遊的鮭魚游近大舟，銜住父親的舵槳——第一次嚇得父親收槳，第二次他緩緩上提，竟連兒子一併提出水面——阿納特克復為人身，此後多年捕獵養家。

sensitivity.note: Godthaab district tale recorded by Rasmussen, 1910s. Human-salmon transformation is part of West Greenland reincarnation belief.

passages.text: There was once an old man who had only one son, called Anarteq, and many daughters, all fond of going out reindeer hunting to the eastward in a fjord. At the base of the fjord Anarteq let his sisters drive the reindeer up the hillside so that the beasts came out into a big lake, where he could row out in his kayak and kill them all; in a few days they had their umiak filled with meat. One day, the reindeer having swum out and Anarteq striking them down, he saw a calf, caught hold of it by the tail and began to play with it — but suddenly the reindeer heaved up its body above the surface of the water and kicked at the kayak so that it turned over. He could not get up, because the kayak was full of water; at last he crawled out of it, and the women on shore could not get out to help him. 'Now the salmon are beginning to eat my belly,' they heard him say, and very slowly he went to the bottom.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Knud Rasmussen, Eskimo Folk-Tales (Worster 1921), 'Anarteq'; not verbatim.

passages.text: When Anarteq woke again to his senses he had become a salmon. His father was obliged to go back alone, and from that time, having no son, he had to go out hunting as if he had been a young man, never again rowing up to those reindeer grounds. Anarteq, now a salmon, went with the others in the spring, when the rivers break up, out into the sea to grow fat. But his father, greatly wishing to go once more to their old hunting grounds, went there again as chief of a party after many years had passed, his daughters rowing for him; and when they came near the base of the fjord he thought of his son and began to weep. His son, coming up from the sea with the other salmon, saw the umiak and his father in it weeping, swam to it, and caught hold of the paddle with which his father steered — and the father, greatly frightened, drew the paddle out of the water, saying: 'Anarteq had nearly pulled the paddle from my hand that time.'
passages.note: Paraphrase of Knud Rasmussen, Eskimo Folk-Tales (Worster 1921), 'Anarteq'; not verbatim.

passages.text: For a long while he did not venture to put his paddle in the water again; when he did at last, he saw that all his daughters were weeping, and a second time Anarteq swam quickly up to the umiak. Again the father tried to draw in his paddle when the son took hold of it, but this time he could not move it — then at last he drew it quite slowly to the surface, in such a way that he drew his son up with it. And then Anarteq became a man again, and hunted for many years to feed his kin.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Knud Rasmussen, Eskimo Folk-Tales (Worster 1921), 'Anarteq'; not verbatim.

texts.period: Inuit oral tradition (Godthaab, West Greenland); collected by Knud Rasmussen, published 1921

source.work: Knud Rasmussen (collector), Eskimo Folk-Tales, ed. and rendered into English by W. J. Alexander Worster (Gyldendal, 1921), 'The Guillemot that could talk', eBook #28932

summary.en: A wifeless man rows north from the south to hear the talking guillemot of the bird cliffs. At the foot of a mightily big cliff his guide points out the nest; the bird comes out, stretches itself very long, stares down at the kayaks, and says quite clearly: 'This, I think, must be that southern man, who has come far from a place in the south to hear a guillemot.' The southerner falls forward on his face, dead of fright. Buried below the nest, he has no grave-marker but the bird's; and his widowless crew winter there, fed by him — his soul, the teller hints, still catching fish for the umiak's women until they keep him south as a husband.
summary.zh: 無妻男子自南方北行，只為一聽傳說中會說話的海鳩。巨大鳥崖之下，嚮導指向鳥巢；海鳩出巢，伸長身子俯瞰皮艇，清楚說道：『想必這就是那位南方人，不遠千里來聽海鳩說話。』南方人撲面倒地，活活嚇死。他被葬於鳥巢之下；其大舟上的婦人們在此過冬，靠『他』捕魚為生——次年南歸時，眾人不肯放他北返，無妻的他遂在南方娶妻成家。

sensitivity.note: Godthaab district tale recorded by Rasmussen, 1910s. Talking-bird motif; the teller's joke about the dead man procuring food marks the tale's comic-macabre register.

passages.text: A man from the south heard one day of a guillemot that could talk, to be found somewhere in the north, and set off northward, toiling along in an umiak. At a village he asked the way — 'Three days' journey away you will find it' — stayed only the night, went on, and at the next village one of the men offered to be his guide. They rowed until they came in sight of a mightily big bird cliff, and at its foot the guide said: 'Here, here is the nest of that guillemot bird.' The man prepared to be very careful when the bird came out; it came out, went to the side of the cliff, stared down at the kayaks, stretching its body to make it very long, and sitting up there said quite clearly: 'This, I think, must be that southern man, who has come far from a place in the south to hear a guillemot.'
passages.note: Paraphrase of Knud Rasmussen, Eskimo Folk-Tales (Worster 1921), 'The Guillemot that could talk'; not verbatim.

passages.text: The bird had hardly spoken when the guide saw that the man from the south had fallen forward on his face, dead — having died of fright at hearing the bird speak. There being no other thing to be done, he covered up the body at the foot of the cliff below the guillemot's nest, went home, and told the others of his place; and the umiak and its crew of women stayed there and wintered in that place. Next summer, when they were making ready to go southward again, they had no man to go with them — but on the way that wifeless man procured food for them by catching fish, and when he had caught enough to fill a pot, he rowed in with his catch.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Knud Rasmussen, Eskimo Folk-Tales (Worster 1921), 'The Guillemot that could talk'; not verbatim.

passages.text: In this way he led them southward. When they came to their own country, they had grown so fond of him that they would not let him go northward again — and so that wifeless man took a wife from among those women, because they would not let him go away to the north. It is said that the skeleton of that wifeless man lies there in the south to this day.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Knud Rasmussen, Eskimo Folk-Tales (Worster 1921), 'The Guillemot that could talk'; not verbatim.

title.en: Kanagssuaq, Who Shared His Catch with Kiliteraq
title.zh: 卡納克舒克與基利特拉克的雪中義氣

texts.period: Inuit oral tradition (Godthaab, West Greenland); collected by Knud Rasmussen, published 1921

source.work: Knud Rasmussen (collector), Eskimo Folk-Tales, ed. and rendered into English by W. J. Alexander Worster (Gyldendal, 1921), 'Kanagssuaq', eBook #28932

summary.en: Icebound and starving on a little island, Kanagssuaq carries his kayak on his head across the floes through snow and heavy sea, and from that day never comes home without a catch. Out in blinding weather he meets Kiliteraq, the only other hunter to venture out, gives him the whole belly skin and blubber to chew, makes his tow-line fast for him through breaking waves, and rows off into the thickly falling snow. When spring comes and the guillemots are driven together, Kiliteraq comes south to find him and pays the debt with a beaded walrus-hide tow-line and a worked bearskin seat — 'Here is that which shall thank you for that service.'
summary.zh: 海冰封島、糧盡之際，卡納克舒克頂著皮艇踏冰出海，頂風冒雪獵豹而歸，此後再無空手之日。暴風雪中他遇上唯一敢出門的獵手基利特拉克，割下整片豹腹皮請他咀嚼油脂，又在碎浪中為他繫好拖繩，然後駛入大雪消失。春至群獵海鳩時，基利特拉克南來尋他，以串珠海象皮拖繩與熊皮座墊相贈——『這些是為謝你那次相助。』

sensitivity.note: Godthaab district tale recorded by Rasmussen, 1910s. Hunter's reciprocity ethic presented as told in the source.

passages.text: Kanagssuaq went out from his own place to live on a little island, and took to wife the only sister of many brothers. Once the cold became so great that the sea between the islands was icebound, and they could no longer go out hunting; at last they had used up their store of food, and all remained lying down from hunger and weakness. Once, when there was open water to the south where they often caught seal, Kanagssuaq took his kayak on his head and went out hunting, rowing out in a northerly wind with snow falling and a heavy sea; he came upon a number of black seal but struck only a little fjord seal, which came up between him and the others — easier to cut up, he said. When he had got this seal he took his kayak on his head again and went home across the ice, his house-fellows shouting for joy at the little creature he sent sliding in; next day he caught two black seal, and after that never went out without bringing home something.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Knud Rasmussen, Eskimo Folk-Tales (Worster 1921), 'Kanagssuaq'; not verbatim.

passages.text: The north wind and the snow and the cold continued, and when he lay out waiting for seal he often wished he might meet Kiliteraq, the great hunter from another place, the only one who would venture out in such weather. Great dearth of food had come also to Kiliteraq's place, and he took his kayak on his head and went out across the ice; coming some way, he sighted Kanagssuaq, who had already made his catch and was getting his tow-line out. As soon as he came up, Kanagssuaq cut away the whole of the belly skin and gave it to him, and Kiliteraq, desiring blubber greatly, took good big pieces to chew. When black seal came up, Kanagssuaq bade him row in to where they were; Kiliteraq harpooned one and killed it on the spot — but as he wound up the harpoon line, a breaking wave rolled down and hid the kayak utterly; the bladder showed behind it, then the kayak with paddles held in balancing position. A second wave washed over him as he tried the tow-line again.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Knud Rasmussen, Eskimo Folk-Tales (Worster 1921), 'Kanagssuaq'; not verbatim.

passages.text: Coming up, he said: 'I am now so far out that I cannot make my tow-line fast. Will you do this for me?' Kanagssuaq made his tow-line fast, and as soon as the seal was in tow, Kiliteraq rowed away in the thickly falling snow and was soon lost to sight; when he came home, his many comrades were filled with great thankfulness towards him. A few days later the snow was falling only far away on the horizon, the weather became fine, and in spring they hunted guillemots, driving them together in flocks.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Knud Rasmussen, Eskimo Folk-Tales (Worster 1921), 'Kanagssuaq'; not verbatim.

passages.text: One day, amid the killing and loading, a kayak came in sight on the sunny side — Kiliteraq — who thrust his way through the kayaks to Kanagssuaq, stuck his paddle in between the thongs, drew out from behind his kayak opening a splendid tow-line of walrus hide beautifully worked with many beads of walrus tooth, and a second time a piece of bearskin fashioned to the seat of a kayak. These he gave to Kanagssuaq, saying: 'Once in the spring, when I could not make my tow-line fast to a seal, you helped me, and made it fast. Here is that which shall thank you for that service.' And then he rowed away.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Knud Rasmussen, Eskimo Folk-Tales (Worster 1921), 'Kanagssuaq'; not verbatim.
